title: Venus' Coronae: 3D Maps Reveal a Planet More Active Than We Knew
summary: Venus, often called Earth's twin, hides a turbulent interior beneath its thick clouds. Its surface is dotted with 741 coronae—huge rings of fractures that can stretch over 2,100 km across, like Artemis Chasma, which could blanket the U.S. from Denver to the West Coast. For decades, scientists puzzled over these formations. Now, Anna Gulcher of the University of Freiburg and her team have used old Magellan spacecraft data to create innovative 3D models, presented at the European Geosciences Union's 2026 General Assembly. 'Coronae display extraordinary diversity,' Gulcher says. 'They do not represent a single formation mechanism, but instead reflect a spectrum of dynamic processes.' The models combine gravity and topography data with geodynamic simulations, identifying possible warm mantle upwellings beneath 52 coronae. This is perhaps the strongest evidence that different plume-related tectonic processes occur there. 'We think they are formed by something circular in shape from the interior,' Gulcher explains. 'A magma plume, hotter than surrounding material, causes uplift of the crust, creating these rings.' The findings hint that Venus may be more active than current gravity data can detect. The study also sheds light on why Venus lacks Earth-style plate tectonics. Earth's oceans hydrated rocks, making them weaker and more pliable, allowing plates to form and recycle carbon. Venus, bone-dry, likely never had large oceans, so its lithosphere remained stiff. 'On Earth, carbon is recycled back into the mantle very efficiently,' Gulcher notes. Without this, Venus couldn't stabilize its climate. Upcoming missions like VERITAS and EnVision will map coronae in unprecedented detail, potentially revealing whether Venus ever had a chance at habitability.
why_it_matters: Understanding why Venus turned into a scorching hothouse while Earth stayed habitable helps us grasp the delicate balance of climate and plate tectonics, offering a cautionary tale for our own planet's future as we change its atmosphere.

background_read: Venus, the second planet from the Sun, is often called Earth's twin because of its similar size and density, but it evolved in a drastically different way — a scorching hothouse with surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead.
NASA's Magellan spacecraft, which arrived at Venus in 1990, used radar to peer through the thick clouds and revealed a landscape dotted with strange ring-like features, later named coronae.

Anna Gulcher, a researcher at the University of Freiburg in Germany, presented the new 3D models at the European Geosciences Union (EGU) General Assembly, a major annual conference for Earth and space scientists, using that decades-old Magellan data in a novel way.

The upcoming NASA VERITAS mission (planned for the late 2020s) and ESA's EnVision orbiter (2030s) will return to Venus with much sharper instruments, able to see through the clouds and map coronae with precision unimaginable in Magellan's time.

This research is important not only for Venus but also for understanding Earth: if our planet's oceans hydrated the crust and made plate tectonics possible, then a dry Venus shows how crucial water is for maintaining a stable climate over billions of years.

perspectives.description: Gulcher's team demonstrated how old data can yield breakthrough discoveries when paired with modern computer models. This 'second life' for Magellan observations shows that you don't always need a new spacecraft to make fundamental progress in planetary science.

The 3D models depend on low-resolution gravity maps collected decades ago. Critics might worry that the warm upwelling signals could be misinterpreted, and only a new generation of sensors — like those on VERITAS — can truly confirm whether coronae are linked to active plumes.

The stark contrast between Venus and Earth highlights how a seemingly small difference — the presence of surface water — can set a planet on a completely different geological path. This study reinforces that plate tectonics is not a given, even for Earth-sized worlds.

The VERITAS and EnVision missions, arriving in the next decade, could map coronae with 100 times better resolution. If they confirm widespread plume activity, it would mean Venus is still geologically alive — a stunning possibility that would shift the focus of future exploration toward understanding its interior.
